title: in their own words where they exist
word: in their own words where they exist
hook: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off: the warning Gargi got in a king's hall, and the two questions she came back with
carry: in their own words where they exist
tomorrow: in their own words where they exist

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last of Lal Ded: too much gets you nowhere, too little makes you proud, and in measure the doors open. Did you stop at enough? Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

Don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. That's a line from an Upanishad, said in a king's hall in front of a crowd of learned men, to a woman who wouldn't stop asking questions. Her name is Gargi. She falls silent. And later, in the same debate, she stands up again. Akka and Lalla left sayings of their own. Other women's words did not survive at all. And some, like Gargi, speak inside a text that is mostly about someone else. Today, where their words exist, we listen to them.
screen: `DON'T ASK TOO MUCH.` → `A WOMAN WHO KEEPS ASKING.` → `HER WORDS INSIDE ANOTHER STORY.`

segments.voice: The text is the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad. King Janaka of Videha has called the wise to his court, and the sage Yajnavalkya is answering all comers. Gargi steps forward. Her question, in paraphrase: all this world is woven back and forth on water, like threads on a loom. So on what is water woven? On wind, he says. And wind? On the sky. She keeps going, layer after layer, each answer becoming her next question. Then Yajnavalkya stops her. Gargi, don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. You are asking too far about a deity that is not to be asked about like this. And Gargi falls silent. It's easy to stop there, as if she lost. The text doesn't. Later, after another sage has questioned him and been answered, she rises again. She says to the assembly, in paraphrase: I will ask him two questions. If he can answer them, none of you will beat him. And the Upanishad gives her a striking picture. She comes at him like a warrior from Kashi or Videha, stringing an unstrung bow and taking up two arrows that can pierce. Her questions: that which is above the sky and below the earth, between them, past, present and future, on what is it woven? And that, on what is it woven? He answers: in space. And space, on what is that woven? This time the answer goes deeper than wind and water, to the imperishable, the one that sees and is not seen. Gargi turns to the assembly and tells them none of them will beat him. Notice what carries the debate to its deepest answer. Not only his replies. Her questions.
screen: `A DEBATE IN KING JANAKA'S HALL` · `ON WHAT IS IT WOVEN?` · `DON'T ASK TOO MUCH` · `TWO ARROWS, TWO QUESTIONS`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: Gargi's question. Sit, and let the breath slow. Look at one thing near you: a cup, a hand, the floor. Ask quietly, what holds this up? Let an answer come. Then ask the same of that answer. What holds that up? Don't hurry. When you reach the place where no answer comes, don't push. Rest there, in the question, the way Gargi did when she fell silent. If you pray, you can rest there before God. The bell holds the time.
In their own words, where they exist. Today, Gargi in the Upanishad, warned not to ask too much, who came back with two questions like arrows. Today's word.
Your line: in their own words where they exist. Today, when someone says don't ask, notice the question, and keep it, for the right moment. Day one thousand three hundred sixty-seven.

fork.setup: you're Gargi. the sage has just warned you: don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. what do you do?

original.note: Sanskrit. Gargi, the questioner in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

trapdoor: what you thought: in the old texts, only men ask the big questions.
what it means: in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Gargi questions Yajnavalkya in a king's hall, twice.
what a scholar hears: a woman's words kept inside a text about a man's debate, and the debate's sharpest turn shaped by her two questions.
recall: asked who would leave a sleeping wife
asks to see her sons once more

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.6 (Gargi: on what is water woven … 'do not ask too much, lest your head fall off')
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.8 (Gargi's two questions, the warrior with two arrows, the imperishable)

notes: Max Müller's 1884 translation of the Brihadaranyaka (SBE 15) is public domain, but its exact wording could not be verified, so everything is paraphrased.

BU 3.6: confirm the chain (water, wind/air, sky/atmosphere, onward) and the warning, which the text gives as 'do not ask too much, lest your head fall off', about a deity not to be asked about too much.

BU 3.8: confirm the warrior of Kashi or Videha image, the two questions (above the sky, below the earth, between, past/present/future: on what woven?), the answers (space; the imperishable, akshara) and Gargi's verdict that none will defeat him.
Editor pass: fixed 'after others have tried' (BU 3.7 has one questioner, Uddalaka) and added the intermediate answer (space) before the imperishable per BU 3.8; rewrote a garbled closing line.
